FLAT: Formal Languages as Types.author: Fengmin Zhu and Andreas Zeller
FLAT: Formal Languages as Types.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
FLAT: Formal Languages as Types.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
FLAT: Formal Languages as Types.title: FLAT: Formal Languages as Types
FLAT: Formal Languages as Types.abstract: Programmers regularly use strings to encode many types of data, such as Unix file paths, URLs, and e-mail addresses. They are conceptually different, but existing mainstream programming languages treat them as the same string type . This is problematic: the type system allows, for instance, malicious HTML text to be passed to a function expecting an e-mail address. To distinguish conceptually different string types and to avoid potential vulnerabilities, we regard formal languages as types (FLAT) , thereby restricting the set of valid strings using context-free grammars and, if needed, semantic constraints. Applying this type-based approach, we offer a unified solution for string API documentation, input validation, malicious input detection, language-based fuzzing, and test oracles, all at once, based on user-annotated FLAT and, if necessary, pre- and post-conditions. We implement this idea and present FLAT-PY, a testing framework for Python. By attaching annotations directly to Python code, FLAT-PY automatically performs runtime type checking via code instrumentation and reports any detected type errors as soon as possible. We conducted case studies on real Python code fragments: FLAT-PY can detect logical bugs from random inputs generated by a language-based fuzzer, relying on a reasonable number of user annotations.

JIT-DCK: A KAN Multi-Task Model for Just.author: Jingwei Wang and Chenchen Li and Shenglin Wang and Hui Li and Furui Zhan and Ning Qiao and Shikai Guo
JIT-DCK: A KAN Multi-Task Model for Just.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
JIT-DCK: A KAN Multi-Task Model for Just.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
JIT-DCK: A KAN Multi-Task Model for Just.title: JIT-DCK: A KAN Multi-Task Model for Just-In-Time Code Defect Prediction and Localization
JIT-DCK: A KAN Multi-Task Model for Just.abstract: In software quality assurance, Just-In-Time Defect Prediction (JIT-DP) and Just-In-Time Defect Localization (JIT-DL) automate the identification of potential defective code and localization of defect lines by analyzing program change characteristics and code commit contexts. These techniques enable just-in-time quality monitoring and defect prevention during development, while also reducing manual costs and improving reliability. Due to the high dynamism and unstructured noise in code change data within agile development scenarios, as well as the difficulty in capturing complex nonlinear synergistic effects of multidimensional expert features, existing work faces dual challenges: lack of data robustness and lack of fine-grained modeling of expert features. To address these challenges, we propose a multi-task interaction technology JIT-DCK , which contains three core components: defect feature preprocessing component, defect prediction component, and defect localization component. The defect feature preprocessing component creates a subword vocabulary, controls extreme values and removes interference to generate data with three aspects, sending the line-level structure to the defect localization component and the semantic aggregation and expert features to the defect prediction component. The defect prediction component is structured with a three-layer cooperative architecture. It works on fusing semantic and line-level features and also models the complex nonlinear relationships of 14-dimensional expert features to achieve effective defect prediction. The defect localization component builds a closed-loop decision chain. It integrates commit-level global features and line-level local semantics through multi-level encoding and dynamic attention mechanisms for accurately localizing defects. Experiments show that JIT-DCK significantly outperforms SOTA models in defect prediction and localization metrics such as F1-Score + 2.76%, AUC + 1.79%, CodeChurn@20%Recall + 2.88%, Top5-Acc + 3.10%, Top10-Acc + 2.55%, Recall@20%CodeChurn l + 6.46%, CodeChurn@20%Recall l + 18.58%, and IFA + 3.57%, demonstrating its competence in code defect prediction and localization tasks.

Towards an Oracle for Binary Decompositi.author: Ang Jia and He Jiang and Zhilei Ren and Xiaochen Li and Zhipeng Yang and Yaxin Duan and Ming Yu Fan and Ting Liu
Towards an Oracle for Binary Decompositi.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Towards an Oracle for Binary Decompositi.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Towards an Oracle for Binary Decompositi.title: Towards an Oracle for Binary Decomposition Under Compilation Variance
Towards an Oracle for Binary Decompositi.abstract: Third-Party Library (TPL) detection, which identifies reused libraries in binary code, is critical for software security analysis. At its core, TPL detection depends on binary decomposition—the process of partitioning a monolithic binary into cohesive modules. Existing decomposition methods, whether anchor-based or clustering-based, fundamentally rely on the assumption that reused code exhibits similar function call relationships. However, this assumption is severely undermined by Function Call Graph (FCG) variations introduced by diverse compilation settings, particularly different function inlining decisions that drastically alter FCG structures. In this work, we conduct the first systematic empirical study to establish the oracle for optimal binary decomposition under compilation variance. We first develop a labeling method to create precise FCG mappings on a comprehensive dataset compiled with 17 compilers, 6 optimizations, and 4 architectures; then, we identify the minimum semantic-equivalent function regions between FCG variants to derive the ground-truth decomposition. This oracle provides the first rigorous evaluation framework that quantitatively assesses decomposition algorithms under compilation variance. Using this oracle, we evaluate existing methods and expose their critical limitations: they either suffer from over-splitting failure or over-merging failure. This highlights the urgent need for compilation-aware decomposition approaches.

RustC 4 ++: Improving Rust Code-Comment.author: Yichi Zhang and Yang Feng
RustC 4 ++: Improving Rust Code-Comment.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
RustC 4 ++: Improving Rust Code-Comment.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
RustC 4 ++: Improving Rust Code-Comment.title: RustC 4 ++: Improving Rust Code-Comment Inconsistency Detection via Hybrid LLM and Static Analysis
RustC 4 ++: Improving Rust Code-Comment.abstract: Maintaining consistency between source code and its associated comments is essential for software reliability, maintainability, and user experience, particularly in the Rust programming ecosystem, where comments serve as both developer guidance and an authoritative API contract. However, existing automated inconsistency detection approaches are largely tailored for object-oriented languages and fall short of addressing Rust’s unique features, such as explicit panic semantics, trait-based abstraction, and idiomatic use of option and finiteness constraints. In this article, we introduce RustC 4 ++, a novel hybrid framework that integrates large language model (LLM)-driven constraint extraction, static program analysis, and SMT-based bidirectional verification to detect and diagnose code-comment inconsistencies in Rust. RustC 4 ++ extends previous solutions by supporting a richer taxonomy of constraints, including interval, boundary, existence, option, and finiteness constraints, and pioneers a systematic method for propagating comment constraints across trait and implementation boundaries. Leveraging chain-of-thought prompt engineering, RustC 4 ++ robustly interprets natural language comments, maps it to formal specifications, and checks their alignment with code logic through precise static analysis and formal reasoning. We conduct extensive experiments on 17 diverse, real-world Rust projects, demonstrating that RustC 4 ++ substantially outperforms prior tools in both precision and recall, and is capable of uncovering subtle, actionable inconsistencies that have led to confirmed fixes in upstream repositories. By elevating comments to enforceable, verifiable contracts, RustC 4 ++ not only enhances code quality and comment reliability in the Rust ecosystem but also offers generalizable techniques and insights for automated code comment analysis in other modern programming languages.

Automatically Checking Semantic Equivale.author: Viktor Malík and Tomáš Vojnar and František Nečas
Automatically Checking Semantic Equivale.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Automatically Checking Semantic Equivale.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Automatically Checking Semantic Equivale.title: Automatically Checking Semantic Equivalence between Versions of Large-Scale C Projects
Automatically Checking Semantic Equivale.abstract: Motivated by existence of software projects that undergo regular refactorings and modifications and yet need to ensure semantic stability of some of their core parts, we propose a highly scalable approach for automatically checking semantic equivalence of different versions of large-scale, real-world C projects, with a particular (though not exclusive) focus on the Linux kernel. The proposed method uses a novel combination of pattern matching with light-weight static analysis and control-flow transformations. The method checks preservation of the semantics of functions forming the API of the project being analysed as well as of the semantics of its global variables, which typically hold various control parameters. For the latter, a specialised slicing procedure is proposed to slice out code influenced by these variables and concentrate the analysis on that code only. Although the method cannot prove equivalence on heavily refactored code, it can compare thousands of functions in the order of minutes while producing a low number of false non-equality verdicts as our experiments show. The method has been implemented over the LLVM infrastructure in a tool called DiffKemp . Our results show that DiffKemp , unlike other existing tools, gives practically useful results even on projects of the size of the Linux kernel.

Evaluating the Effectiveness of Deep Lea.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Evaluating the Effectiveness of Deep Lea.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Evaluating the Effectiveness of Deep Lea.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Deep Learning Models for Foundational Program Analysis Tasks
Evaluating the Effectiveness of Deep Lea.abstract: While deep neural networks provide state-of-the-art solutions to a wide range of programming language tasks, their effectiveness in dealing with foundational program analysis tasks remains under explored. In this article, we present an empirical study that evaluates four prominent models of code (i.e., CuBERT, CodeBERT, GGNN, and Graph Sandwiches), plus four popular large language models (i.e., GPT3.5 , GPT-4o mini , Qwen2.5-Coder , and DeepSeek Coder ), in two such foundational tasks: (1) alias prediction, in which models predict whether two pointers must alias, may alias, or must not alias; and (2) equivalence prediction, in which models predict whether or not two programs are semantically equivalent. At the core of this study is CodeSem , a dataset built upon the source code of real-world flagship software (e.g., Linux Kernel, GCC, MySQL) and manually validated for the two prediction tasks. Results show that all models are accurate in both prediction tasks. We also conduct a comprehensive, in-depth analysis of the results of all models in both tasks, concluding that deep learning models are generally capable of performing foundational tasks in program analysis, even though in specific cases their weaknesses are also evident. Our code and evaluation data are publicly available at https://github.com/CodeSemDataset/CodeSem .

Not-So-Pretty: Studying and Segmenting M.author: Jianchen Zhao and Kundi Yao and Masanari Kondo and Hetong Dai and Weiyi Shang and Yasutaka Kamei
Not-So-Pretty: Studying and Segmenting M.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Not-So-Pretty: Studying and Segmenting M.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Not-So-Pretty: Studying and Segmenting M.title: Not-So-Pretty: Studying and Segmenting Multiline Console Logs
Not-So-Pretty: Studying and Segmenting M.abstract: Console logs play a crucial role in the development, maintenance, and operation of software systems. However, their diverse and human-oriented formatting presents significant challenges for automated analysis. Most existing log analysis benchmarks and the tools built upon them operate under the assumption that individual log messages correspond to single lines. In reality, console logs frequently span multiple lines and exhibit a wide range of structures and formats, complicating parsing and downstream analysis. In this article, we conduct a qualitative study on a diverse dataset of console logs, identifying 4 structural types and 10 common formats in multiline log segments. We find that although only 3% of the log messages are multiline, they account for 66% of the content by line count. To address the challenge of parsing log messages that span multiple lines, we also propose a deep learning-based preprocessing approach that splits logs into structurally and semantically consistent segments and assigns labels about their format. Our model, trained on a manually labelled dataset, achieves an F1 score of 0.88 for log segmentation and 0.84 for log format classification. We release our dataset and model to support further research in log analysis.

SparseTG-GS: Test Case Generation via Sp.author: Shunhui Ji and Yunhe Li and Yan Xiao and Hai Dong and LiMing Hu and Pengcheng Zhang
SparseTG-GS: Test Case Generation via Sp.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
SparseTG-GS: Test Case Generation via Sp.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
SparseTG-GS: Test Case Generation via Sp.title: SparseTG-GS: Test Case Generation via Sparse Perturbation Group
SparseTG-GS: Test Case Generation via Sp.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have been widely applied in the field of computer vision. While DNNs exhibit remarkable accuracy in classification tasks, they remain susceptible to adversarial examples. Robustness testing for DNNs has become crucial. Existing test case generation methods suffer from certain limitations, such as dispersed distribution of perturbations, insufficient realism, and high time cost. This article proposes a test case generation method, Sparse Perturbation-Based Test Case Generation—Group-Wise Sparsity (SparseTG-GS). Initially, superpixel segmentation is applied to partition the input image into multiple superpixels. Next, perturbation groups are iteratively introduced into the superpixels until the perturbed image effectively compromises the target DNN. Finally, based on the importance of each perturbation, the initial perturbation scheme is improved by re-adding perturbation groups and minimizing superfluous perturbations and perturbation magnitudes. We improve the AdvGAN framework to construct the Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for calculating a perturbation importance matrix for test cases with enhanced optimization efficiency. Experimental study shows that the test cases generated by SparseTG-GS achieve the best attack success rate for target DNNs. The perturbed superpixels in the test cases are fewer and more interpretable. In addition, SparseTG-GS is efficient for generating test cases, especially on large-sized images. The code of SparseTG-GS is available at https://github.com/Yunhelee/SparseTG-GS .

Adaptive Anomaly Detection for Multi-Dim.author: Xu Wang and Minghui Chu and Hongwei Yu and Chuan Wen Luo and Chunming Hu
Adaptive Anomaly Detection for Multi-Dim.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Adaptive Anomaly Detection for Multi-Dim.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Adaptive Anomaly Detection for Multi-Dim.title: Adaptive Anomaly Detection for Multi-Dimensional Issue Reports
Adaptive Anomaly Detection for Multi-Dim.abstract: Modern cloud-native architectures demand automated incident identification systems to identify sparse yet critical attribute combinations in multidimensional issue report data. Therefore, there is a need for automated incident detection systems to perform rapid and accurate anomaly detection. Traditional search-based methods are hindered by the combinatorial explosion of attributes and stringent real-time detection requirements, resulting in inefficiency and poor scalability for anomaly identification in large-scale cloud-native systems. To address these challenges, we propose an Adaptive Anomaly Detection for Multi-Dimensional Issue Reports (AADMIR), a combinatorial optimization framework integrating dynamic operator scheduling with scoring-guided neighborhood expansion. Unlike traditional meta-heuristics, AADMIR introduces three core mechanisms specifically designed for high-dimensional issue analysis: (1) Adaptive Operator Selection: A regression-guided dynamic adjustment strategy that automatically selects optimal search operations based on real-time exploration progress, overcoming the “static strategy trap” in conventional methods. (2) Neighborhood Expansion: A hierarchical second-order neighborhood expansion mechanism addresses the limitations of traditional first-order search by introducing second-order neighborhood. This dynamic topology extends the search scope while maintaining efficiency through probabilistic sampling, effectively balancing global exploration and local exploitation to mitigate local optima entrapment. (3) Regression-Driven Adaptive Judgment: We propose a lightweight, threshold-based evaluation metric that combines mathematical change-point detection with information entropy to quantify tuple benefits. By defining an energy metric and using the normalized change threshold, it robustly distinguishes true anomalies from normal fluctuations, avoids false positives inherent in purely entropy-based methods, and delivers rapid greedy-step decisions with minimal computational overhead. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that AADMIR achieves superior precision, recall, and F1-score compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly excelling in high-dimensional scenarios.

Software Vulnerabilities as Cognitive Bl.author: Matthew Richard Ivory and John Towse and Miriam Sturdee and Mark Levine and Bashar Nuseibeh
Software Vulnerabilities as Cognitive Bl.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Software Vulnerabilities as Cognitive Bl.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Software Vulnerabilities as Cognitive Bl.title: Software Vulnerabilities as Cognitive Blindspots: Assessing the Suitability of a Dual Processing Theory of Decision Making for Secure Coding
Software Vulnerabilities as Cognitive Bl.abstract: Software vulnerabilities are present in many software systems, putting people who entrust software with their data in harm’s way. Many vulnerabilities are avoidable since they are well documented—yet they remain widespread. One explanation for their persistence is they represent software blindspots, problems that are implicit in the mental models of developers and which escape attention. Our current understanding of how attention and decision making influence specific secure coding behaviours is limited, and so, we present a preregistered study to evaluate whether differences in decision making style impact blindspots and the identification of code vulnerabilities. Programmers were given code puzzles to complete, including some that contained vulnerabilities. Participants also competed the cognitive reflection test and measures of rational decision making. We replicate several key predictions from previous blindspot research, map the analysis onto dual-systems research and describe the effect sizes of psychological constructs. We then model data simulations to demonstrate the sampling required for highly powered empirical studies in this domain. We support previous findings that technical or cybersecurity expertise have little impact on the ability to detect vulnerabilities. We argue that dual processing theory helps to interpret security behaviours and the presence of software blindspots.

Evaluation of an Interval-Based Fitness.author: Darina Bajusova and Petr Šilhavý and Radek Šilhavý
Evaluation of an Interval-Based Fitness.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Evaluation of an Interval-Based Fitness.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Evaluation of an Interval-Based Fitness.title: Evaluation of an Interval-Based Fitness Function within SOMA for COCOMO-Based Effort Estimation
Evaluation of an Interval-Based Fitness.abstract: This study introduces a fitness function, Predictions Within Individuals’ Intervals (PII [Lo, Hi] ), designed to optimize software effort estimation (SEE) tasks within the Self-Organizing Migrating Algorithm (SOMA). The effectiveness of the PII [Lo, Hi] fitness function is evaluated and compared against well-known fitness functions, including MAE, MSE, MMRE, PRED(0.25), and MMER. In addition to fitness-function-level comparisons, the study further benchmarks models calibrated using the PII [Lo, Hi] fitness function against Quantile Regression (QR) and Quantile Regression with Gradient Boosting (QRGB). The evaluation uses the Constructive Cost Model (COCOMO) on the NASA18, Kemerer, Miyazaki94, and ISBSG datasets. The study employs evaluation metrics, statistical testing, residual analysis, and convergence analysis to validate the results. The findings show that MAE and PII [−10, 25] produced stable and accurate predictions, while MSE and MMER demonstrated higher variability. Residual and convergence analyses further support the robustness of PII [−10, 25] , though its performance declined in one scenario (TEST 3), warranting further refinement. The results were also supported by the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and Win-tie-loss performance analyses. Future research will focus on extending the applicability of the PII [Lo, Hi] fitness function and exploring its interaction with different optimization algorithms, as well as investigating the potential of automated parameter tuning.

How Safe Are AI-Generated Patches? A Lar.author: Amirali Sajadi and Kostadin Damevski and Preetha Chatterjee
How Safe Are AI-Generated Patches? A Lar.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
How Safe Are AI-Generated Patches? A Lar.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
How Safe Are AI-Generated Patches? A Lar.title: How Safe Are AI-Generated Patches? A Large-scale Study on Security Risks in LLM and Agentic Automated Program Repair on SWE-bench
How Safe Are AI-Generated Patches? A Lar.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks are increasingly used for development tasks such as automated program repair (APR). Prior work has identified security risks in LLM-generated code, but most studies focus on synthetic, simplified, or isolated tasks. We present a large-scale security analysis of LLM-generated patches using 20,000+ GitHub issues from SWE-bench. We evaluate developer-written patches, two standalone LLMs (Llama 3.3 Instruct-70B and GPT-5.4 nano), and four agentic frameworks (OpenHands, AutoCodeRover, HoneyComb, and SWE-agent). We also analyze code, issue, and project-level factors associated with insecure patches. Under our evaluated SWE-bench setup, Llama 3.3 introduced 135 manually confirmed vulnerabilities across the train and test sets, compared with 12 in developer-written patches for the same issues. On the SWE-bench test set, GPT-5.4 nano introduced 3 vulnerabilities compared with 2 in developer patches. All four evaluated agentic frameworks also introduced vulnerabilities. OpenHands had the highest retained count, with 44 vulnerabilities across 11 issue instances. Vulnerabilities are associated with broader code modifications and with issues missing specific information. These results suggest that APR systems require proactive risk assessment methods that consider both generated code and issue context.

LRASGen: LLM-based RESTful API Specifica.author: Sida Deng and Rubing Huang and Man Zhang and Chenhui Cui and Dave Towey and Rongcun Wang

LRASGen: LLM-based RESTful API Specifica.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
LRASGen: LLM-based RESTful API Specifica.title: LRASGen: LLM-based RESTful API Specification Generation — RCR Report
LRASGen: LLM-based RESTful API Specifica.abstract: This Replicated Computational Results (RCR) Report accompanies our TOSEM paper “LRASGen: LLM-based RESTful API Specification Generation”. LRASGen is the first framework to use Large Language Models (LLMs) for generating OpenAPI Specifications (OASs) directly from RESTful API source code, without requiring compilation or a runtime environment. The framework is organized as a six-step pipeline that includes endpoint entry file identification, endpoint entry code extraction and cleaning, endpoint method identification, parameter and response identification, parameter constraint identification, and OAS generation. To mitigate LLM hallucination, LRASGen employs three safeguards: structured-output enforcement , cross-validation across three LLMs , and a code-anchor mechanism . Evaluated on 53 real-world RESTful APIs spanning five programming languages and ten frameworks, LRASGen generated accurate specifications (e.g., 99.4% of endpoint methods) and covered, on average, 43.54% more entities than developer-provided specifications, outperforming the state-of-the-art technique, Respector, on all four identification tasks. To support replication, we released the source code, the enhanced ground truth (GT*), the generated specifications, and the experiment scripts. We also packaged the artifact as a Docker image, which needs no local Python installation. We archived the artifacts on Zenodo with a permanent DOI.

MisAbort: Detecting Pseudo-Abortive Bugs.author: Haoran Wang and Shuqiao Zhang and Ming Yuan and Xi Xiao and Tingting Yin and Xinyu Yu and Chao Zhang and Zhiyuan Jiang and Jin Wei
MisAbort: Detecting Pseudo-Abortive Bugs.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
MisAbort: Detecting Pseudo-Abortive Bugs.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
MisAbort: Detecting Pseudo-Abortive Bugs.title: MisAbort: Detecting Pseudo-Abortive Bugs in Windows Kernel Binaries
MisAbort: Detecting Pseudo-Abortive Bugs.abstract: Abortive functions are commonly employed in the Windows kernel to prevent further execution on critical failures. However, some non-abortive functions bear confusing names that mislead developers into believing they will abort. we denoted them as pseudo-abortive functions. Invoking pseudo-abortive functions to handle critical errors introduces pseudo-abortive bugs . These bugs form a distinct class of error-handling weaknesses that have not been systematically modeled, rooted in the semantic mismatch between the caller's intent (i.e., requiring abortion) and the callee's functionality (i.e., no abortion). Detecting such bugs is challenging in binaries , as callers’ intent and callees’ semantics are obscure. To this end, we present MisAbort , a novel binary analysis technique that detects pseudo-abortive bugs in Windows by analyzing callee functionality and caller intent. MisAbort first classifies Windows kernel functions as abortive or non-abortive callees. For non-abortive callees, it isolates suspicious callsites via rule-based caller intent filtering. For these filtered callsites, it then applies a customized machine language model to infer callers’ abortive intent. Finally, MisAbort uses a caller-callee bug assessment to assess the influence of intent-functionality mismatches. We implement a prototype of MisAbort and evaluate it on Windows kernel binaries. MisAbort identifies 85 newly confirmed pseudo-abortive bugs with 13 CNNVD IDs assigned.

Software Engineering for Large Language.title: Software Engineering for Large Language Models: Research Status, Challenges, and the Road Ahead
Software Engineering for Large Language.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has redefined artificial intelligence (AI), pushing the boundaries of AI research and enabling unbounded possibilities for both academia and industry. However, LLM development faces increasingly complex challenges throughout its lifecycle, while existing research has not systematically investigated these challenges and solutions from the perspective of software engineering (SE) approaches. To fill the gap, we systematically analyze the research status throughout the LLM development lifecycle, which is divided into six phases: requirements engineering, dataset construction, model development and enhancement, testing and evaluation, deployment and operations, and maintenance and evolution. We conclude by identifying the key challenges in each phase and presenting potential research directions to address them. In general, we provide valuable insights from an SE perspective to facilitate future advances in LLM development.

Isolating Compiler Bugs through Compilat.author: Yujie Liu and Mingxuan Zhu and Shengyu Cheng and Dan Hao
Isolating Compiler Bugs through Compilat.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Isolating Compiler Bugs through Compilat.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Isolating Compiler Bugs through Compilat.title: Isolating Compiler Bugs through Compilation Steps Analysis
Isolating Compiler Bugs through Compilat.abstract: Compilers are essential to software systems, and their bugs can propagate to dependent software. Ensuring compiler correctness is critical. However, isolating compiler bugs remains challenging due to the internal complexity of compiler execution. Existing techniques primarily mutate compilation inputs to generate passing and failing tests, but often lack causal analysis of internal steps, limiting their effectiveness. To address this limitation, we propose CompSCAN, a novel compiler bug isolation technique that applies analysis over the sequence of compilation steps. CompSCAN follows a three-stage process: (1) extracting the array of compilation steps that leads to the original failure, (2) identifying bug-causing steps and collecting corresponding compiler code elements, and (3) calculating suspicious scores for each code element and outputting a suspicious ranking list as the bug isolation result. We evaluate CompSCAN on 185 real-world LLVM and GCC bugs. Results show that CompSCAN outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both effectiveness and efficiency. CompSCAN successfully isolates 50, 85, 100, and 123 bugs within the Top-1/3/5/10 ranks, respectively. Compared with ETEM and ODFL, two state-of-the-art compiler bug isolation techniques, CompSCAN achieves relative improvements of 44.51% / 50.18% / 36.24% / 24.49% over ETEM, and 31.58% / 49.12% / 44.93% / 21.78% over ODFL on those metrics. Moreover, CompSCAN runs faster on average per bug than both baselines.

Fine-Grained Reasoning Enhanced Vulnerab.title: Fine-Grained Reasoning Enhanced Vulnerability Patch Generation with Multi-View Fix Knowledge
Fine-Grained Reasoning Enhanced Vulnerab.abstract: With the rapid advancement of deep learning, numerous large language models (LLMs) have been developed, achieving remarkable performance across a wide range of code generation tasks. However, in the domain of vulnerability patch generation, existing approaches suffer from two critical limitations: (1) limited reasoning capability, which hampers the modeling of fine-grained fix logic; and (2) insufficient utilization of fix knowledge, with minimal consideration of vulnerability intent. To address these challenges, we propose FraMe, a novel automated approach that integrates F ine-g r ained re a soning paths with M ulti-vi e w fix knowledge to enhance LLM-based vulnerability patch generation. FraMe consists of two modules: stepwise fix-reasoning path collection and multi-view knowledge augmented patch generation. The first module extracts detailed vulnerability–fix context and constructs augmented prompt templates to generate stepwise fix-reasoning paths, enabling the model to capture fine-grained fix logic. The second module leverages multi-view fix knowledge from a vulnerability knowledge graph to model vulnerability intent and supplement code semantics, thereby facilitating the selection of effective few-shot examples and enabling the LLM to generate more accurate patches. We evaluated FraMe on a widely used real-world C/C++ vulnerability dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that FraMe consistently outperforms both existing prompting methods and non-LLM-based techniques, achieving an improvement of 9.4% in the Correct metric at a beam size of 10 compared with the best baseline. The source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/VulDet/FraMe .

A Timed Obstruction Logic for Dynamic Ga.author: David Cortés and Jean Leneutre and Vadim Malvone and James Ortiz
A Timed Obstruction Logic for Dynamic Ga.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
A Timed Obstruction Logic for Dynamic Ga.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
A Timed Obstruction Logic for Dynamic Ga.title: A Timed Obstruction Logic for Dynamic Game Models
A Timed Obstruction Logic for Dynamic Ga.abstract: Securing computational systems within vital infrastructures, such as healthcare, aviation, and energy grids, against malicious attacks is an increasingly difficult challenge. Specially, provably secure systems are often required given the strict guarantees provided by formal methods. However, adversarial threats faced by these critical systems are highly sophisticated, needing verification methods that account for temporal constraints and dynamic interactions. While Timed Game Theory has recently emerged as a robust theoretical foundation for modeling attacker-defender dynamics, it often lacks the expressive power to capture complex real-time properties without prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we introduce Timed Obstruction Logic (TOL), an extension of Obstruction Logic (OL) for verifying timed games with real-time objectives in dynamic models. TOL formally defines interactions where players’ actions influence the underlying system model, capturing essential timed properties required for cyber defense. Furthermore, we propose and implement a PSPACE-complete verification algorithm for TOL, achieving significantly higher expressiveness without exceeding the complexity bounds of classical timed temporal logics. Finally, we benchmarked our implementation against multiple case studies, confirming its potential viability for verifying real-time constraints in cybersecurity scenarios.

Generating Mitigations for Downstream Pr.author: Zirui Chen and Puhua Sun and Xing Hu and Xin Xia and Xiaohu Yang
Generating Mitigations for Downstream Pr.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Generating Mitigations for Downstream Pr.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Generating Mitigations for Downstream Pr.title: Generating Mitigations for Downstream Projects to Neutralize Upstream Library Vulnerability
Generating Mitigations for Downstream Pr.abstract: Third-party libraries are essential in software development as they prevent the need for developers to recreate existing functionalities. However, vulnerabilities within these libraries pose significant risks to dependent projects. Upgrading dependencies is infeasible when no patched version is available or when downstream projects have strict version constraints. Moreover, repairing the vulnerability proves challenging when the source code of the library is inaccessible. State-of-the-art automatic vulnerability repair and automatic program repair methods both fail to address this issue. Therefore, mitigating library vulnerabilities without access to source code or available patches is crucial for a swift response to potential security attacks. Existing tools encounter challenges concerning generalizability and functional security. Upon vulnerability disclosure, Lumen prepares a pool of candidate mitigation strategies by retrieving explicit workarounds from public sources and supplementing the pool with generated strategies based on vulnerability reproduction behavior. Lumen then selects a suitable strategy, autonomously gathers repository-specific context, and adaptively generates a validated mitigation patch. We evaluate Lumen on 474 impacted functions associated with 94 vulnerabilities. Lumen successfully mitigates 393 functions, achieving a success rate of 82.91%, which substantially outperforms the adapted baseline in blocking vulnerability reproduction under our exploit-based evaluation. Additionally, our ablation study evaluates the contributions of strategy composition, strategy selection, and repository-level context collection. Further evaluations show that Lumen can mitigate vulnerabilities disclosed after the knowledge cutoff of the base model.

Detecting JavaScript Libraries on the We.author: Sungmin Park and Seojin Kim and Ben Swierzy and Jihyeok Park
Detecting JavaScript Libraries on the We.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Detecting JavaScript Libraries on the We.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Detecting JavaScript Libraries on the We.title: Detecting JavaScript Libraries on the Web using Property-Order Graphs
Detecting JavaScript Libraries on the We.abstract: Detecting front-end JavaScript libraries is essential for website profiling, vulnerability detection, and dependency management. However, bundlers transpile code in various ways, altering its original structure and complicating detection. State-of-the-art techniques detect libraries at runtime by matching property patterns exposed through the global object. They therefore miss libraries inaccessible from the global object, and identify versions only when version labels are exposed or property-level differences are large. More recent approaches inspect the bundled source, but either target a single bundler or require the target library as input. We present Debun, a scalable technique for detecting JavaScript libraries and their versions using function-level fingerprints. Our key insight is that bundlers preserve property names and the execution order of property operations. We introduce the property-order graph (POG), which captures this order within a function body, and make it robust to interprocedural transformations such as function inlining through preprocessing. To detect partially imported libraries caused by tree shaking, we propose a dependency-aware scoring function. Evaluations on 68 high-traffic websites with 78 libraries show that Debun outperforms five state-of-the-art tools, achieving a 94.64% F1-score in library detection and identifying 88 of the 98 ground-truth versions at the patch level.

Ensuring Gas Optimisation Correctness by.author: Manoel Villarim and Juliano Iyoda and Márcio Cornélio and Alexandre Mota
Ensuring Gas Optimisation Correctness by.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Ensuring Gas Optimisation Correctness by.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Ensuring Gas Optimisation Correctness by.title: Ensuring Gas Optimisation Correctness by Behavioural Equivalence
Ensuring Gas Optimisation Correctness by.abstract: Gas consumption has a financial impact on executing Ethereum smart contracts, making gas optimisation an essential development concern. Although several optimisation techniques exist, applying them can alter contract behaviour, compromising correctness or introducing vulnerabilities. This work introduces a formal verification framework to ensure that gas-optimised contracts remain behaviourally equivalent to their originals. Our approach relies on the Certora Prover to mechanise correctness checking: a transformation rule is selected from our catalogue, applied to a Solidity contract, and verified in Certora. If an optimisation violates equivalence, counterexamples guide a diagnosis and correction. To support practical adoption, we compiled a catalogue of 31 gas-saving transformation rules, each featuring a formal pattern and an example alongside a Certora specification for automated verification. Building this catalogue revealed that two previously published optimisations require updates for Solidity 0.8.0 or superior. To evaluate practical applicability, we conducted a case study on the widely-adopted AAVE V3 DeFi protocol, applying our refinement-based methodology to formally prove the behavioural equivalence of optimised versions against the original. Although not fully automated, the framework is mostly mechanisable. Our results demonstrate that combining formal verification with gas-optimisation strategies is both feasible and effective for real-world smart contracts.

Beyond Methods: An Empirical Study of Fi.author: Guoqing Wang and Mincan Li and Yifan Zhao and Zhihao Gong and Dan Hao
Beyond Methods: An Empirical Study of Fi.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Beyond Methods: An Empirical Study of Fi.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Beyond Methods: An Empirical Study of Fi.title: Beyond Methods: An Empirical Study of File-Level Production-Test Co-evolution and Its Implications for Automation
Beyond Methods: An Empirical Study of Fi.abstract: The co-evolution of production and test code is a critical yet challenging software maintenance activity. However, a persistent paradigm gap exists in the literature. While the identification of co-evolution is advancing to a realistic file-level scope, the automation of test updates predominantly remains focused on an oversimplified method-level view. To bridge this gap, we conduct the first multi-project, empirically grounded taxonomy of file-level change propagation patterns that also quantifies the automation paradigm gap using representative tools. We construct a dataset of over 300,000 co-evolution pairs from 128 Java projects and perform a qualitative analysis on a statistically justified sample set. Our analysis yields a comprehensive, hierarchical taxonomy of four high-level Change Propagation Patterns that explains the mechanisms of file-level co-evolution. It reveals that simple one-to-one method changes—the primary target of current tools—constitute only a minority (2.15%) of cases. Our quantitative analysis then measures the profound impact of this gap. We show that the operational scope of state-of-the-art, method-level automation tools covers only a fraction of these real-world patterns, resulting in a performance mismatch of up to 69% when applied to the broader file-level context. Our work provides both a new theoretical lens and a challenging public benchmark to steer the community towards building the next generation of automation tools that address how co-evolution happens in practice.

To See is Not to Master: Teaching LLMs t.author: Yitong Zhang and Chengze Li and Ruize Chen and Guowei Yang and Xiaoran Jia and Yijie Ren and Jia Li
To See is Not to Master: Teaching LLMs t.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
To See is Not to Master: Teaching LLMs t.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
To See is Not to Master: Teaching LLMs t.title: To See is Not to Master: Teaching LLMs to Use Private Libraries for Code Generation
To See is Not to Master: Teaching LLMs t.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for code generation, yet they remain limited in private-library-oriented code generation, where models are expected to generate code that correctly invokes APIs from private libraries. Existing approaches primarily rely on retrieving private-library API documentation and injecting the retrieved knowledge into the context at inference time. However, our study shows that this strategy is insufficient: even when provided with accurate required API knowledge, LLMs still struggle to invoke private-library APIs effectively . To address this limitation, we propose PriCoder, an approach that improves LLMs’ ability to invoke private-library APIs through automatically synthesized training data. Specifically, PriCoder uses a synthesis graph to organize private-library data synthesis and applies two complementary operations: ❶ Progressive Graph Evolution , which improves data diversity by progressively synthesizing more complex and diverse training samples from basic ones, and ❷ Multidimensional Graph Pruning , which improves data quality through an automatic filtering pipeline. To support rigorous evaluation, we construct two new benchmarks based on recently released libraries that are unfamiliar to the evaluated models. Across the two private-library benchmarks and all evaluated models, PriCoder improves over Vanilla by 13.53–31.66 percentage points in pass@k . On HumanEval and MBPP, PriCoder generally achieves higher performance than RAG-based baselines.

Enhancing Neural Code Representation Wit.author: Huy Gia Nguyen and Christoph Treude and Patanamon Thongtanunam
Enhancing Neural Code Representation Wit.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Enhancing Neural Code Representation Wit.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Enhancing Neural Code Representation Wit.title: Enhancing Neural Code Representation With Additional Context
Enhancing Neural Code Representation Wit.abstract: Automated program comprehension underpins many software engineering tasks, from code summarisation to clone detection. While recent deep learning models have achieved strong results, they typically rely on source code alone and overlook other information that developers routinely use to understand programs, such as version history or structural relationships. This gap limits the ability of current models to capture the broader context in which code evolves and operates. To address this, we conduct an empirical study of how enriching code representations with these additional contextual signals affects the performance of neural models on key program comprehension tasks. We evaluate four downstream software engineering tasks, code clone detection, code classification, code summarisation, and vulnerability detection, using SeSaMe (1,679 semantically similar Java methods from 11 open-source projects), CodeSearchNet (2,117 projects; 63,259 methods paired with natural-language documentation), and Vul4J (178 vulnerability-inducing methods). To ensure a robust comparison, we fine-tune five foundational code models (tree-based and pre-trained Transformer architectures), namely CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, CodeT5, PLBART, and ASTNN, under both code-only and context-augmented settings. We further expand the evaluation to seven code-specialised large language models (CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B, Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B/7B/14B, and DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B), comparing prompt-based context injection against fine-tuned use of context. Experimental results show that context improves classification performance for all five foundational models and, after fine-tuning, for most of the seven LLMs. For summarisation, the effect depends on the model family: version history improves all four foundational models on every metric, whereas context injected into the prompt of a decoder-only LLM helps two of the seven models (Qwen2.5-Coder 7B and 14B, via call-graph context) and lowers both lexical and semantic metrics for the other five. In particular, encoding version history never hurts and usually improves clone detection across the five foundational models (up to +15.92% F1 for CodeT5) and summarisation (e.g., GraphCodeBERT +5.56% METEOR; CodeT5 +3.05% BLEU-4). By contrast, call-graph context delivers model- and task-dependent gains. Combining multiple types of context (version history, call graphs, and method age) can further enhance improvements, reaching up to +21.48% macro-F1 in code classification and +15.04% F1 in clone detection for specific models under concatenation-based aggregation. Finally, a human evaluation with two annotators on 100 Java snippets (rank-ordering with ties evaluation) showed that context-augmented summaries were ranked significantly higher than summaries from models that rely on source code only for Accuracy and Content Adequacy (Wilcoxon \(p\leq 0.026\) ; Cliff's \(\lvert\delta\rvert\) up to 0.55), while improvements in Conciseness were context-dependent; inter-rater agreement was high (Kendall's \(\tau_{b}\) ). Our study highlights the potential benefit of utilising rich and diverse context to enhance the code comprehension capability of neural-based models. An exploratory evaluation on vulnerability detection provides initial evidence that context-enriched representations transfer to security-oriented tasks. It also opens new research directions for optimising contextual encoding strategies in software engineering, for instance automated bug localisation, where call-graph context helps trace fault propagation paths [68].

FeatOutline: Feature-Oriented Repository.author: Yifeng Zhu and Xutian Li and Xianlin Zhao and Zexiong Ma and Kunze Li and Haizhuo Yuan and Yanzhen Zou and Bing Xie

FeatOutline: Feature-Oriented Repository.title: FeatOutline: Feature-Oriented Repository Summarization for Enhanced Code Comprehension and Maintenance
FeatOutline: Feature-Oriented Repository.abstract: Repository-level code summaries are typically organized around directories and files, making functionality that spans multiple artifacts difficult to see and trace to its implementation. We present FeatOutline, a feature-oriented repository summarization approach that organizes a repository around its functionality and connects each generated feature directly to the methods that implement it. FeatOutline combines structural dependencies and semantic similarity to form functionally cohesive groups at the file and method levels, synthesizes these groups into features, and organizes related features into epics. Comparative experiments on eight open-source Java repositories demonstrate that FeatOutline captures documented functionality more completely and traces generated features to source code more accurately. A controlled maintenance study with 16 participants further shows that FeatOutline increases task success by 28.1 percentage points and reduces completion time by approximately one-third relative to a state-of-the-art repository summarization approach. These findings demonstrate that organizing repository code around method-grounded features provides developers with a more effective way to understand, navigate, and maintain unfamiliar repositories.

Black-Box Mutation Testing of Web APIs.author: Lixin Xu and Juan Carlos Gómez Alonso and Alberto Martin-Lopez and Ana B. Sánchez and Huayao Wu and Changhai Nie and Sergio Segura
Black-Box Mutation Testing of Web APIs.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Black-Box Mutation Testing of Web APIs.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Black-Box Mutation Testing of Web APIs.title: Black-Box Mutation Testing of Web APIs
Black-Box Mutation Testing of Web APIs.abstract: The key role of web Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) in software integration has led to a surge in the development of test case generation tools for web APIs. Most of these tools work in black-box mode, without access to the source code, and are primarily assessed based on their ability to detect crashes and violations of API descriptions. As a result, their effectiveness in identifying other types of failures (e.g., incorrect outputs caused by functional bugs) remains largely unknown. In this article, we propose a black-box mutation testing approach to assess the fault-detection capabilities of testing tools for web APIs. Unlike traditional mutation testing, which introduces faults in the source code, our approach generates faulty but realistic variants of HTTP responses, simulating the observable effects of bugs in the underlying implementation. These mutated responses can then be used to evaluate the effectiveness of testing tools in detecting incorrect outputs, making our approach readily applicable to both closed- and open-source web APIs. The approach is implemented in an extensible tool, HttpMutator , which supports 23 mutation operators for HTTP responses, including mutations on status codes, headers, and JSON payloads. Evaluation results on 30 API operations from 19 open-source and industrial APIs show that HttpMutator is effective in generating diverse and realistic erroneous outputs, with a positive correlation between black-box and white-box mutation coverage. More importantly, HttpMutator has already proven instrumental in assessing the effectiveness of test case generation tools for REST APIs, highlighting its practical relevance.

Agentic Software Engineering: Foundation.author: Ahmed E. Hassan and Hao Li and Dayi Lin and Bram Adams and Tse-Hsun Peter Chen and Yutaro Kashiwa and Dong Qiu
Agentic Software Engineering: Foundation.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Agentic Software Engineering: Foundation.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Agentic Software Engineering: Foundation.title: Agentic Software Engineering: Foundational Pillars and a Research Roadmap
Agentic Software Engineering: Foundation.abstract: Agentic Software Engineering (SE 3.0) represents a new era where intelligent agents are tasked not with simple code generation, but with achieving complex, goal-oriented SE objectives. To harness these new capabilities while ensuring trustworthiness, we must recognize a fundamental duality within the SE field in the Agentic SE era, comprising two symbiotic modalities: SE for Humans and SE for Agents. This duality demands a radical reimagining of the foundational pillars of SE (actors, processes, tools, and artifacts), which manifest differently in each modality. This new vision of SE requires two distinct, purpose-built workbenches (aka tools) for these two collaborative modalities: the Agent Command Environment (ACE), a command center where humans orchestrate, mentor, and oversee agent teams while managing an inbox of agent-generated events like Merge-Readiness Packs (MRPs) and Consultation Request Packs (CRPs); and the Agent Execution Environment (AEE), a digital workbench where agents not only execute tasks but can proactively invoke human expertise when facing complex trade-offs or ambiguity. This bidirectional partnership, which supports agent-initiated human callbacks and handovers, gives rise to new, structured engineering activities (i.e., processes) that redefine human-AI collaboration, elevating the practice from agentic coding to true agentic software engineering. This paper presents the Structured Agentic Software Engineering (SASE) vision, outlining several of the foundational pillars for the future of SE. The paper culminates in a research roadmap that identifies a few key challenges and opportunities while briefly discussing the resulting impact of this future on SE education. Our goal is not to offer a definitive solution, but to provide a conceptual scaffold with structured vocabulary to catalyze a community-wide dialogue, pushing the SE community to think beyond its classic, human-centric tenets toward a disciplined, scalable, and trustworthy agentic future.

The Impact of AI Coding Assistants on So.author: Annie Vella and Kelly Blincoe
The Impact of AI Coding Assistants on So.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
The Impact of AI Coding Assistants on So.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
The Impact of AI Coding Assistants on So.title: The Impact of AI Coding Assistants on Software Engineering: A Longitudinal Study
The Impact of AI Coding Assistants on So.abstract: AI coding assistants have become prolific in recent years. Through a longitudinal mixed-methods investigation, we examined how professional software engineers perceive the effects of AI coding assistants in regard to task focus, developer experience, and productivity. Two questionnaires were administered six months apart, yielding 158 eligible participants at the first time point, 101 at the second, and a matched longitudinal cohort of 95. Participants reported spending less time on most development tasks, with 82% reporting less on writing code. We found a broader shift in focus from creation to verification activities. We propose a new category of work we term supervisory engineering work , encompassing the direction, evaluation, and correction of AI output. This construct is broader than the extra review overhead that has been previously reported in literature since it encompasses directing and shaping AI output both before and during creation. We also identified a productivity-experience paradox: consistently positive productivity perceptions alongside eroding developer experience. These findings suggest that AI coding assistants may be reshaping both the nature of software engineering work and how engineers experience it.

\"Like Taking the Path of Least Resistan.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
\"Like Taking the Path of Least Resistan.title: "Like Taking the Path of Least Resistance": Exploring the Impact of LLM Interaction on the Creative Process of Programming
\"Like Taking the Path of Least Resistan.abstract: As AI takes on more of the generative work that once required human imagination, despite documented limitations in creative ability, a critical question emerges: How does GenAI affect users’ creativity? Through a within-subject study followed by retrospective interviews with (N=20) programmers, we investigated the impact of LLMs on participants’ process of creative thinking in programming and the creativity of generated solutions. Across two conditions (LLM-assisted vs. unassisted), participants using LLMs had significantly shorter idea-generation periods ( \(p=1.6\times 10^{-5}\) ) and fewer creative moments ( \(p=4.4\times 10^{-7}\) ). Qualitative analysis of participants’ interactions and interviews revealed four different human-LLM collaboration modes supporting various problem-solving strategies. However, a comparative analysis of the generated solutions shows that while LLMs can help generate more correct and functional code, LLM-assisted solutions to algorithmic tasks were significantly more similar to one another, even though the number of unique ideas was comparable. Based on our findings, we discuss design implications and considerations for effectively using LLMs to support user creativity.

Unpacking Bias in LLMs: A Causal Testing.title: Unpacking Bias in LLMs: A Causal Testing Perspective
Unpacking Bias in LLMs: A Causal Testing.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) – the backbone of modern Natural Language Processing applications (NLP) - are notoriously subject to biases that reflect stereotypes present in their training. Fairness testing typically aims to expose bias by generating texts that should yield equivalent outputs, yet differ only in protected attributes such as gender or religion. However, fairness testing for LLMs is more complex than it seems. Bias depends not only on variations in the protected attribute, but also on its causal interactions with non-protected attributes and their combined influence on the output. Ignoring these dependencies risks producing unrealistic scenarios or misleading conclusions about bias. We introduce CFTA ( Causal Fairness Testing and Analysis ), a causality-driven technique for generating test datasets that uncover multiple forms of bias while enabling fine-grained decomposition of (real or apparent) bias-inducing paths. We evaluate CFTA on nine LLMs on a sentiment analysis task, exposing contributions of both obvious and hidden biases between models.

What to Retrieve? Investigating Effectiv.title: What to Retrieve? Investigating Effective Call Information in Repository-level Code Generation
What to Retrieve? Investigating Effectiv.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) emerges as a widely adopted solution in repository-level code generation by retrieving functions for direct reuse or learning similar usage patterns. Nevertheless, it remains unexplored which types of contexts effectively assist LLMs. In this paper, we categorize the context of function calls and empirically analyze the performance of LLMs. Specifically, we define call information along two dimensions: call depth , including direct-level , inward expansion (to callees), and outward expansion (to callers), as well as call granularity , including function-level , module-level , and file-level . We investigate the utility of the context in two distinct scenarios: precision-oriented call extraction and relevance-oriented call retrieval , targeting precise call information and relevant call information , respectively. We conduct comprehensive experiments with three mainstream LLMs on two widely used benchmarks, CoderEval and DevEval. When precise call information is provided, the additional inclusion of inward expansion, outward expansion, module-level, and file-level context enhances the average Pass@1 of the studied LLMs by 2.11%, 79.59%, 37.54%, and 82.54%, respectively. When the relevant call information is provided, incorporating the same set of strategies leads to improvements of 18.00%, 4.77%, 26.07%, and 44.60% in average Pass@1, respectively. This empirical study offers practical insights for optimizing RAG strategies in repository-level code generation.

Large Language Models for Cyber Security.author: Hanxiang Xu and Shenao Wang and Ningke Li and Kailong Wang and Yanjie Zhao and Kai Chen and Ting Yu and Yang Liu and Haoyu Wang
Large Language Models for Cyber Security.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology

Large Language Models for Cyber Security.title: Large Language Models for Cyber Security: A Systematic Literature Review
Large Language Models for Cyber Security.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has opened up new opportunities for leveraging AI in a variety of application domains, including cybersecurity. As the volume and sophistication of cyber threats continue to grow, there is an increasing need for intelligent systems that can automatically detect vulnerabilities, analyze malware, and respond to attacks. In this survey, we conduct a comprehensive review of the literature on the application of LLMs in cybersecurity (LLM4Security). By comprehensively collecting over 40K relevant papers and systematically analyzing 185 papers from top security and software engineering venues, we aim to provide a holistic view of how LLMs are being used to solve diverse problems across the cybersecurity domain. Through our analysis, we identify several key findings. First, we observe that LLMs are being applied to an expanding range of cybersecurity tasks, including vulnerability detection, malware analysis, and network intrusion detection. Second, we analyze application trends of different LLM architectures (such as encoder-only, encoder–decoder, and decoder-only) across security domains. Third, we identify increasingly sophisticated techniques for adapting LLMs to cybersecurity, such as advanced fine-tuning, prompt engineering, and external augmentation strategies. A significant emerging trend is the use of LLM-based autonomous agents, which represent a paradigm shift from single-task execution to orchestrating complex, multi-step security workflows. Furthermore, we find that the datasets used for training and evaluating LLMs are often limited, highlighting the need for more comprehensive datasets and the use of LLMs for data augmentation. Finally, we discuss the main challenges and opportunities for future research, including the need for more interpretable models, addressing the inherent security risks of LLMs, and their potential for proactive defense. Overall, our survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art in LLM4Security and identifies several promising directions for future research. We believe that the insights and findings presented in this survey will contribute to the growing body of knowledge on the application of LLMs in cybersecurity and provide valuable guidance for researchers and practitioners working in this field.

A Survey on LLM-Based Code Generation fo.author: Sathvik Joel and Jie JW Wu and Fatemeh H. Fard
A Survey on LLM-Based Code Generation fo.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
A Survey on LLM-Based Code Generation fo.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
A Survey on LLM-Based Code Generation fo.title: A Survey on LLM-Based Code Generation for Low-Resource and Domain-Specific Programming Languages
A Survey on LLM-Based Code Generation fo.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in code generation for popular programming languages. However, their performance in Low-Resource Programming Languages (LRPLs) and Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs) remains a critical challenge. This gap affects millions of developers—with Rust alone having 3.5 million users—who are currently unable to fully leverage LLM capabilities. LRPLs and DSLs face unique challenges, including severe data scarcity and, for DSLs, highly specialized syntax and semantics that are poorly represented in general-purpose datasets. Addressing these challenges is crucial as LRPLs and DSLs significantly enhance development efficiency in specialized domains and applications, including financial and scientific works. While several surveys on LLMs for software engineering and code exist, none comprehensively address the challenges and opportunities specific to LRPLs and DSLs. Our survey fills this gap by providing a systematic review of the current state, methodologies, and challenges in leveraging LLMs for code generation in LRPL and DSL. We filtered 111 papers from over 27,000 published studies from 2020–2024 to understand the capabilities and limitations of LLMs in these specialized domains. We also expanded our literature search to include five recent papers from 2024–2025. We report LLMs used, benchmarks, and metrics to evaluate code generation in LRPLs and DSLs, as well as strategies used to enhance LLM performance, and the collected datasets and curation methods in this context. We identified four main evaluation techniques used in the literature, along with several metrics to assess code generation in LRPL and DSL. We categorized the methods used for LLM improvement into six main groups and summarized the novel methods and architectures proposed by the researchers. We also classified different approaches used for data collection and preparation. While different techniques, metrics, and datasets are used, there is a lack of a standard approach and a benchmark dataset to evaluate code generation in several LRPLs and DSLs. We discuss several distinctions of the studied approaches with the ones used in High-Resource Programming Languages (HRPLs), as well as several challenges unique to these languages, especially DSLs. The challenges stem from the scarcity of data, the unique requirements, and specialized domains, which often need expertise guidelines or domain-specific tools. Accordingly, we provide insights into different research opportunities for the studied aspects. This survey serves as a comprehensive resource for researchers and practitioners working at the intersection of LLMs, software engineering, and specialized programming languages, providing a foundation for future advancements in LRPL and DSL code generation. A GitHub repository was created to organize the papers of this survey at https://github.com/jie-jw-wu/Survey-CodeLLM4LowResource-DSL .

Agentic Much? Adoption of Coding Agents.author: Romain Robbes and Théo Matricon and Thomas Degueule and André Hora and Stefano Zacchiroli
Agentic Much? Adoption of Coding Agents.booktitle: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Agentic Much? Adoption of Coding Agents.journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
Agentic Much? Adoption of Coding Agents.title: Agentic Much? Adoption of Coding Agents on GitHub
Agentic Much? Adoption of Coding Agents.abstract: In the first half of 2025, coding agents have emerged as a category of development tools that have very quickly transitioned to the practice. Unlike “traditional” code completion LLMs such as Copilot, agents like Cursor, Claude Code, or Codex operate with high degrees of autonomy, up to generating complete pull requests starting from a developer-provided task description. This new mode of operation is poised to change the landscape in an even larger way than code completion LLMs did, making the need to study their impact critical. Also, unlike traditional LLMs, coding agents tend to leave more explicit traces in software engineering artifacts, such as co-authoring commits or pull requests. We leverage these traces to present the first large-scale study (128,018 projects) of the adoption of coding agents on GitHub, finding an estimated adoption rate of 22.20–28.66% on February 21st, 2026, which is very high for a technology only a few months old—and increasing. We carry out an in-depth study of the adopters we identified, finding that adoption is broad: it spans the entire spectrum of project maturity; it includes established organizations; and it concerns diverse programming languages or project topics. At the commit level, we find that commits assisted by coding agents are larger than commits only authored by human developers, and have a large proportion of features and bug fixes. These findings highlight the need for further investigation into the practical use of coding agents.
Agentic Much? Agent READMEs: An Empirical Study of Con.title: Agent READMEs: An Empirical Study of Context Files for Agentic Coding
Agent READMEs: An Empirical Study of Con.abstract: Agentic coding tools receive goals written in natural language, break them down into specific tasks, and write or execute code with minimal human intervention. Central to this process are agent context files (e.g., AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md) that provide persistent, project-level instructions. In this article, we conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 2,303 agent context files from 1,925 repositories to characterize their structure, maintenance, and content. We find that these files are not static documentation but complex, difficult-to-read artifacts that evolve like configuration code through frequent, small additions. Our content analysis of 16 instruction types shows that developers prioritize functional context, such as test procedures (75.9%), implementation details (70.8%), and architecture (68.1%). We also identify a significant gap: non-functional requirements such as security (14.8%) and performance (14.5%) are rarely specified. These findings indicate that while developers use context files to make agents functional, they provide few guardrails to ensure that agent-written code is secure or performant, highlighting the need for improved tools and practices.

Improving Google A2A Protocol: Protectin.author: Yedidel Louck and Ariel Stulman and Amit Z. Dvir

Improving Google A2A Protocol: Protectin.title: Improving Google A2A Protocol: Protecting Sensitive Data and Mitigating Unintended Harms in Multi-Agent Systems
Improving Google A2A Protocol: Protectin.abstract: Google’s A2A protocol provides a secure communication framework for AI agents, but it has critical limitations when handling highly sensitive information such as payment credentials and identity documents. These gaps increase the risk of unintended harms, including unauthorized disclosure, privilege escalation, and misuse of private data in generative multi-agent environments. In this article, we identify key weaknesses in A2A: insufficient token lifetime control, lack of strong customer authentication, overbroad access scopes, and missing consent flows. We propose a modular, interceptor-based architecture to address these weaknesses. Our refinements introduce a Zero-Trust Interceptor that enforces explicit consent orchestration, ephemeral scoped tokens, and direct user-to-service data channels to minimize exposure across time, context, and topology. A component-level evaluation of the interceptor’s deterministic enforcement logic, conducted across 5,000 protocol-enforcement trials, demonstrates that the enhanced protocol structurally eliminates the sensitive-data leakage paths covered by the tested checks, yielding a 0% structural success rate under the stated enforcement assumptions and keeping enforcement overhead at the sub-millisecond level. Comparative analysis highlights the advantages of our deterministic, protocol-level enforcement over both the original A2A specification and stochastic model-based safeguards. These contributions establish a practical, statistically validated path for evolving A2A into a privacy-preserving framework for multi-agent systems.

Mapping the Trust Terrain: LLMs in Softw.title: Mapping the Trust Terrain: LLMs in Software Engineering—Insights and Perspectives
Mapping the Trust Terrain: LLMs in Softw.abstract: The application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in Software Engineering (SE) continues to grow rapidly across both industry and academia. As these models become integral to critical SE processes, ensuring their reliability and trustworthiness becomes essential. Achieving this requires a balanced approach to trust: excessive trust can introduce security vulnerabilities, while insufficient trust may hinder innovation. However, the conceptual landscape of trust in LLMs for SE (LLM4SE) remains unclear. Key concepts such as trust, distrust, and trustworthiness lack precise definitions, factors that shape trust formation remain underexplored, and metrics for trust in LLMs remain undeveloped. To clarify the current research landscape and identify future directions, we conducted a comprehensive review of 88 articles: a systematic review of 18 studies on LLMs in SE, supplemented by an analysis of 70 articles from the broader trust literature. Furthermore, we surveyed 25 domain experts to gather practitioners’ perspectives on trust and identify gaps between their experiences and the existing literature. Our findings provide a structured overview of trust-related concepts in LLM4SE, outlining key areas for future research. This study contributes to building more trustworthy LLM-assisted software engineering processes, ultimately supporting safer and more effective adoption of LLMs in SE.

SGAgent : Suggestion-Guided LLM-Based Mu.title: SGAgent : Suggestion-Guided LLM-Based Multi-Agent Framework for Repository-Level Software Repair
SGAgent : Suggestion-Guided LLM-Based Mu.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to the emergence of intelligent agents capable of autonomously interacting with environments and invoking external tools. Recently, agent-based software repair approaches have received widespread attention, as repair agents can automatically analyze and localize bugs, generate patches, and achieve state-of-the-art performance on repository-level benchmarks (e.g., SWE-Bench). However, existing software repair approaches usually adopt a localize-then-fix paradigm , jumping directly from “where the bug is” to “how to fix it,” leaving a fundamental reasoning gap. To this end, we propose SGAgent , a S uggestion- G uided multi- Agent framework for repository-level software repair, which follows a localize-suggest-fix paradigm. Specifically, SGAgent introduces a suggestion to strengthen the transition from localization to repair. The suggester starts from the buggy locations and incrementally retrieves relevant context until it fully understands the bug, and then provides actionable repair suggestions. Moreover, we construct a Knowledge Graph (KG) from the target repository and develop a KG-based toolkit to enhance SGAgent ’s ability to enhance global contextual awareness and repository-level reasoning. Based on these components, three specialized sub-agents in SGAgent (i.e., localizer, suggester, and fixer) collaborate to achieve automated end-to-end software repair. We evaluated SGAgent on the SWE-Bench-Lite benchmark. Experimental results show that SGAgent with Claude-3.5 achieves 51.3% repair accuracy, 81.2% file-level, and 52.4% function-level localization accuracy with an average cost of $1.48 per instance, outperforming all baselines using the same base model. Moreover, SGAgent generalizes well across different base LLMs, further reaching a 60.7% resolution rate with Claude-4. When extended to vulnerability repair, SGAgent achieves a 48.0% resolution rate on VUL4J and VJBench, demonstrating strong generalization across tasks and programming languages.

Scenario-Guided LLM-Based Mobile App GUI.author: Shengcheng Yu and Yuchen Ling and Chunrong Fang and Quan Zhou and Yi Zhao and Chunyang Chen and Shaomin Zhu and Zhenyu Chen
